name: Body dysmorphia & mirror checking

lead: Body dysmorphic disorder is a psychiatric condition in which a person spends hours on perceived flaws in their appearance that others barely notice. Mirror checking, comparing, reassurance seeking and camouflage are typical behaviours, and some people avoid mirrors instead.

Looksmaxxing communities involve heavy self-scrutiny, and critics cited by Wikipedia link the culture to body dysmorphia. No controlled study found establishes how often BDD occurs in these communities.

paras: Clinical models treat checking and similar safety behaviours as maintaining appearance concern. Treatment research focuses on cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and ritual prevention, and on serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

Reviews report significant impairment, frequent comorbid depression and anxiety, and relatively common suicidal ideation. Cosmetic treatment typically does not relieve the distress, according to Wikipedia, and BDD is often underdiagnosed.

lead: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a psychiatric condition marked by persistent preoccupation with perceived defects in appearance that are minor or unnoticeable to others, together with repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, comparing, reassurance seeking and camouflaging [1][2][3]. Mirror checking, along with its opposite, mirror avoidance, is among the best-described of these behaviours [2][4].

In looksmaxxing communities, appearance scrutiny, self-rating and photo comparison are routine, and journalists and researchers have discussed whether these habits overlap with or worsen body dysmorphia. Wikipedia reports that critics describe looksmaxxing as linked to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation [5]; Grokipedia likewise says self-rating and comparison are linked to body dysmorphia, depression and anxiety [6]. The articles do not present controlled studies establishing that looksmaxxing causes BDD.

Clinical reviews describe cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin reuptake inhibitors as the best-supported treatments [3][7]. Reviews also report that people with BDD frequently seek cosmetic or dermatological treatment and that BDD is common in those settings [3][4].

paras: BDD involves preoccupation with a perceived flaw that takes up hours each day and causes distress or impaired functioning. The flaw may be imagined or a slight difference that the person sees as much larger [8]. DSM-5 (2013) reclassified the condition within the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter and recognised muscle dysmorphia as a subtype [1][8].

The Italian psychiatrist Enrico Morselli described the condition as dysmorphophobia in the late nineteenth century. The American Psychiatric Association first included it in DSM-III in 1980 and named it body dysmorphic disorder in 1987 [8].

Clinical reviews list mirror checking, camouflaging with makeup or clothing, excessive grooming, comparing, reassurance seeking and skin picking as typical associated behaviours, with some patients instead avoiding mirrors and social situations [2][7][9][4]. Wikipedia describes both repeated checking and mirror avoidance as signs of the disorder [8].

Cognitive-behavioural models propose that such behaviours, sometimes called safety behaviours, help maintain appearance concern. A randomised experiment with 84 undergraduate women who had elevated appearance concerns tested the effects of reducing appearance-related safety behaviours such as mirror checking and grooming on appearance concerns and related symptoms [10]. Wikipedia reports that the structured CBT manual by Sabine Wilhelm and colleagues includes exposure and ritual prevention [8].

A review in the Icelandic medical journal gives a weighted community prevalence of around 2%, higher in clinical, cosmetic and dermatology settings, with BDD usually beginning in childhood or adolescence and often co-occurring with depression, substance use disorders, social anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder [3]. Wikipedia cites a meta-analysis estimating general-population prevalence at about 17%, and notes that older estimates were 2 to 3 percent, so published figures differ by source and method [8].

Reviews report that BDD is frequently underdiagnosed because patients conceal symptoms out of shame, that insight is often poor, and that suicidal ideation and attempts are relatively common [3][9][4]. An early case series of 30 patients and a series of 33 children and adolescents documented its features [11][12].

Muscle dysmorphia, in which a person believes their body is too small or insufficiently muscular, is a recognised subtype in DSM-5 and mostly affects men [8]. Published studies include a qualitative investigation of its phenomenology [13] and a report on posting muscle photos as a possible body-checking behaviour [14]. A multicentre study has examined BDD among patients with acne [15].

A guide for dermatologists and cosmetic surgeons reports that people with BDD often present to those practitioners, that preoccupation with skin, hair and nose is most common, and that reassurance seeking may be directed at clinicians [4]. Wikipedia says cosmetic treatment typically does not relieve the distress and recommends that surgeons and psychiatrists collaborate to screen candidates [8].

Human research on BDD is extensive; research specific to looksmaxxing communities is not. A randomised experiment tested reducing appearance-related safety behaviours in women with elevated appearance concerns [10]. Reviews state that cognitive behavioural therapy and serotonin reuptake inhibitors are most effective, and one reports that higher doses and longer trials than in depression are often needed [3][7]. No controlled studies found have examined mirror checking or BDD prevalence within looksmaxxing forums.

Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing reports critics who describe the culture as demoralising and linked to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, as well as practitioners who report benefits such as dating success and peer affirmation [5]. Grokipedia also reports concern that self-rating and comparison, and fatalistic narratives about genetics, can deepen distress [6]. A 2026 analysis of dangerous facial-aesthetics trends on social media examined looksmaxxing discourse, though its abstract does not address BDD.

timeline.event: Enrico Morselli describes dysmorphophobia, per Wikipedia [8].
BDD recognised in DSM-III as an atypical somatoform disorder [8].
DSM revision renames it body dysmorphic disorder [8].
DSM-5 moves BDD to the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter [1][8].
